extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, writers, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on poetic craft (borrowing from nature, imagination vs memory, metre), rhetorical aims, and descriptive depiction (space, character) illustrated with analogies from painting and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic borrowing & imaginative transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet ought not to pick nature's pocket: let him borrow, and so borrow as to repay by the very act of borrowing. Examine nature accurately, but write from recollection; and trust more to your imagination than to your memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow from nature, but transform the borrowed material so that the act of borrowing itself repays or enriches the source. Observe nature carefully (accurate examination) but compose from recollection—allow imagination to reshape and elevate memory into art. Anti-pattern: literal transcription of observed details without imaginative reworking ('picking nature's pocket').

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre should be musical, not merely mechanical
rubrics_metrics.description: Really the metre of some of the modern poems I have read, bears about the same relation to metre properly understood, that dumb bells do to music; both are for exercise...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metre as part of musical expression rather than as an athletic or mechanical exercise. Aim for natural, music-like rhythm that serves feeling and sense; avoid metrically correct but lifeless lines that function only as technical practice. Example anti-pattern: verse that scans yet sounds like 'dumb bells'—useful for exercise but not for genuine poetic music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and distinguish rhetorical aims (rhetoric, logic, grammar, rhematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of rhetoric is persuasion,--of logic, conviction,--of grammar, significancy. A fourth term is wanting, the rhematic, or logic of sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the communicative aim of a passage: persuasion (rhetoric), conviction (logical force), or clear signification (grammar). In addition, attend to the 'rhematic' level—the logic of sentence construction and how sentences themselves carry thought. Craft choices should align with which of these aims you intend to achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and sustain a clear authorial/objective purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of Thucydides was to show the ills resulting to Greece from the separation and conflict of the spirits or elements of democracy and oligarchy. The object of Tacitus was to demonstrate the desperate consequences of the loss of liberty on the minds and hearts of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing (especially historical or argumentative prose), identify the central object or thesis you wish to show and shape the work around that demonstrative purpose. Keep the narrative and evidence focused on illustrating the chosen consequence, cause, or moral; avoid wandering aims that dilute the central demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict space and atmosphere with attention to 'air' and distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the remarkable difference between Claude and Teniers in their power of painting vacant space. Claude makes his whole landscape a plenum: the air is quite as substantial as any other part of the scene... Never did any one paint air, the thin air, the absolutely apparent vacancy between object and object, so admirably as Teniers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In description, render not only objects but the space between them—the atmosphere, distances, and the sense of vacancy or plenitude. Avoid compressing every element to the same plane (which creates a suffocating effect); instead, use tonal, spatial, and lexical cues to create believable depth and 'thin air' where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform mundane details into a magnificent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: He extracts the latent poetry out of these common objects,--that poetry and harmony which every man of genius perceives in the face of nature... he throws them into a vast and magnificent whole, consisting of heaven and earth and all things therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinary, everyday details as the raw material for poetic elevation. The craft is to handle humble images as they occur in nature and assemble them so their combined effect reveals a larger, latent poetry. Anti-pattern: treating everyday elements as trivial ornament rather than sources of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between idealization and particular realism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italian masters differ from the Dutch in this--that in their pictures ages are perfectly ideal. The infant that Raffael's Madonna holds in her arms cannot be guessed of any particular age; it is Humanity in infancy. The babe in the manger in a Dutch painting is a fac-simile of some real new-born bantling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide stylistically whether you will idealize characters (make them types or embodiments of an idea) or portray them as specific, particular individuals. Both approaches are legitimate but yield different effects: idealization universalizes meaning; particular realism grounds the work in concrete specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray inward humanity, not merely external marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraits by the old masters... are pictures of men and women: they fill, not merely occupy, a space; they represent individuals, but individuals as types of a species. Modern portraits... give you not the man, not the inward humanity, but merely the external mark, that in which Tom is different from Bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim in character-writing to convey inner life and typifying humanity rather than only surface identifiers or fashionable external traits. Avoid reducing characters to distinguishing marks or mere physical/fashionable differences; instead, render behaviors, feelings, and moral/psychological depth that make them feel like full human beings.
